What “low to medium” risk on a Fund Facts sheet actually means

How Canadian mutual fund risk ratings are calculated from ten years of monthly returns, and what each level can look like in a single year in dollars. Three charts and an editable fund example.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read a Fund Facts risk rating as a range of yearly outcomes

Interactive planning lab

Fund Facts risk level for this standard deviationLow to medium
About two years in three: one-year return between-4% and 14%
About 19 years in 20: one-year return between-13% and 23%
A bad year (2 standard deviations below average) on your amount-$6,500

Fund Facts risk levels come from the 10-year standard deviation of monthly returns, annualised, under National Instrument 81-102 Appendix F. The ranges here assume returns spread roughly like a bell curve around the average you enter; real markets have more extreme years than this assumption suggests, so treat the 19-in-20 range as a floor for how bad a year can be, not a limit. A risk level describes past volatility, not the chance of loss or future returns.

The central idea

A Fund Facts risk rating measures how much a fund’s returns have bounced around over ten years. “Low to medium” still allows losing years: with a 9% standard deviation and a 5% average, a fall of 13% or more is a plausible bad year.

01

Where the rating comes from

Every mutual fund sold in Canada publishes a two-page Fund Facts document with a risk rating on a five-step scale: low, low to medium, medium, medium to high and high. Since 2017 fund managers must use one standard method. They calculate the fund's standard deviation—how widely its returns have swung around their own average—from the most recent ten years (120) of monthly returns, expressed per year, and place it in a band:

CSA risk-classification bands (NI 81-102 Appendix F)
Standard deviationRisk level
0 to under 6Low
6 to under 11Low to medium
11 to under 16Medium
16 to under 20Medium to high
20 or greaterHigh

A fund without ten years of history uses a reference index for the missing period. A manager may rate a fund higher than its band if that is reasonable, but not lower.

02

Turning a percentage into a year you can picture

Standard deviation is easier to read as a range. If yearly returns spread roughly like a bell curve, about two years in three land within one standard deviation of the average and about 19 years in 20 within two. Take a fund with a 9% standard deviation—“low to medium”—and an assumed 5% average return. Two years in three would fall between −4% and 14%; 19 in 20 between −13% and 23%. On CAD 50,000, a year two standard deviations below average is a loss of about CAD 6,500.

The chart repeats that arithmetic for a fund near the middle of each band. A “medium to high” fund with an 18% standard deviation could see a bad year near −31%; a “high” fund near −43%.

03

What the rating does not tell you

  • It looks backwards. Ten calm years can give a low rating to a fund that could still fall sharply.
  • Real markets have fatter tails. Very bad years happen more often than a bell curve suggests, so treat the 19-in-20 range as a guide, not a floor.
  • It measures ups and downs equally. A fund that jumps up is “riskier” on this scale than one that drifts down slowly.
  • Other risks are separate. Interest-rate sensitivity, currency, concentration and liquidity are described in the fund's prospectus and Fund Facts text, not in the five-step scale.
  • Band edges are blunt. A fund at 10.9% and one at 11.1% get different labels despite nearly the same volatility.

04

Using the rating with your risk profile

The fund rating describes the product; your risk profile describes you. A suitable recommendation connects the two through the whole account, not one fund at a time—several low-to-medium funds can still add up to more stock exposure than you expect, and one higher-rated fund can fit a cautious account in a small amount. When you read a Fund Facts sheet, look at the rating together with the “How has the fund performed?” section, which shows its actual best and worst three-month returns.

This guide explains a calculation. It does not rate or recommend any fund.
